verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster: Do not destroy. Of David. A miktam. When Saul sent, and they watched the house to put him to death.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to a tune that begs, Do not destroy. David's song, a miktam, from the night Saul sent his men, and they took up their watch around the house, waiting for the dawn that would let them kill him.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a headnote, and it is the only stage direction the psalm gets. It tells the performers where David stands: inside his own house, with armed men outside it, and a king's order behind them. The story is in 1 Samuel 19:11-17. Saul's men are told to watch the house overnight and kill David in the morning, and Michal lets him down through a window. Rashi reads the verb the same way, tying the watching to Michal's report that David was ill, and Meiri says the psalm was composed once David had escaped. Metzudat David adds the purpose: the men guard the house so he cannot slip away in the dark. Note the verb. Hebrew shamar, 'to watch, to guard', is what the hunters do here, and it comes back in verse 10 as David's own answer: 'to you I will watch', where the same root turns the guard on God. The echo in verse 18 does not repeat it: there the same line ends 'I will sing' (zamar), so the watching resolves into song. The KJV leaves אַל תַּשְׁחֵת as the unexplained 'Altaschith', as if it were a tune name only, and shows 'chief Musician' for the choirmaster; the Hebrew is a plain command, 'do not destroy', which Rashi hears as the psalm's name from a man close to death pleading for mercy. It may also point to a melody, as with Psalm 57 and 58, and the text does not settle it. The KJV also softens 'to put him to death' to 'kill him'; Hebrew lahamito is a causative, an execution ordered by authority, not a brawl. Miktam is of uncertain meaning; the KJV simply transliterates 'Michtam'. In Hebrew numbering this title is verse 1, so the KJV verse numbers in the rest of the psalm run one behind.

philological_notes.note: 'Do not destroy', a negative command from the verb shachat. It heads Psalms 57, 58, 59 and 75. It may name a melody, or it may be the plea itself; the plain sense is kept here.
'And they watched, kept guard': the hunters' verb, which David turns toward God in verse 10, 'to you I will watch' (אֶשְׁמֹרָה).
A causative infinitive, 'to cause him to die, to put him to death', which names the aim of the watch as an execution, not a chance death.

verses.translation_literal: Deliver me from my enemies, my God; from those rising up against me set me on high.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pull me out of their reach, my God. Out of the hands of my enemies, out from under those who rise against me, lift me up where they cannot climb.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first word is an imperative thrown across a closed room: 'Deliver me.' The speaker is a man inside a house with armed men outside; the plea is physical before it is theological.

The last verb, 'set me on high', is the root of misgav, the high, unreachable place of a fortress, and it prepares the refrain 'my refuge' in verses 10 and 17. The KJV's 'defend me' flattens it. Hebrew has a picture: lift me beyond the walls and out of the enemy's reach. Ibn Ezra notes that David was in a low place, which makes the elevation concrete.

philological_notes.note: Piel of sagav, 'to be high, inaccessible'; here 'set me out of reach'. The same root gives misgav, 'refuge, high fortress', in verse 10.

token_glosses.gloss: from those rising up against me

verses.translation_literal: Deliver me from workers of iniquity, and from men of bloods save me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Save me from the men who make a trade of wrong, from the men whose hands are always red.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two plural nouns do the work: 'workers of iniquity' and 'men of bloods'. The Hebrew for 'blood' here is plural, damim, the usual idiom for blood that is shed, so bloodguilt rather than gore. The KJV's 'bloody men' is archaic and hits the wrong note; they are men of murder, who do wrong as a craft.

Radak and Ibn Ezra take both phrases as the same men, the watchers sent to kill. Malbim assigns the two phrases to two sets of enemies, those who whisper against him and those who rise to murder him.

philological_notes.note: 'Men of bloods': the plural damim means blood that is shed, so bloodguilt. The English 'bloody men' of the KJV misses that these are killers, not simply violent.

verses.translation_literal: For behold, they lie in wait for my life; fierce ones stir up strife against me; not my transgression and not my sin, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look: they are lying in wait for my life. The fierce ones gather against me. It is not for any crime of mine, not for any sin of mine, LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Behold' makes God a witness: the speaker points at the street. 'My nefesh' is the life itself, the throat and breath, not a spirit, so the KJV's 'my soul' hides the threat. They ambush a person.

The verb yaguru is the hard one. The KJV's 'are gathered' follows Ibn Ezra and Radak, who read it as 'gather'; Rashi reads it as 'lodge' (they stay in my house to guard me). The sense of stirring up quarrels (gur) is possible too. The final cry, 'not my transgression and not my sin', is a claim of innocence before Saul, not before God, with 'YHWH' placed last for weight; the plea is that no wrong of David's explains this.

philological_notes.note: Disputed. 'Gather' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri), 'lodge' (Rashi, those who stay in the house to watch), or 'stir up strife'. The English versions follow 'gather'.
'My life, my throat': nefesh is the living self. The KJV's 'soul' suggests something spiritual; the danger is bodily.

verses.translation_literal: Without iniquity they run and set themselves ready; awake to meet me, and see.
verses.translation_dramatic: There is no wrong in me, and still they run and take their places. Wake, and come to meet me. See it with your own eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Without iniquity' is ambiguous: it is probably 'though I have no guilt', with beli as a negative before 'iniquity' in the sense of 'my guilt'. The KJV's 'without my fault' supplies the 'my'; the YLT's 'without punishment' misses the point. The speakers who run are the pursuers, preparing themselves ('set themselves ready'; Radak notes the reflexive form is shortened).

The two imperatives are strong: 'Awake' calls on a God who seems asleep, a motif the psalm repeats in verse 6, and 'see' echoes the verb of verses 10 and 11, where David will see his enemies. Ibn Ezra links 'awake' to the watching of verse 1: the watchers do not sleep, so God must not.

philological_notes.note: From kun, 'to be firm, ready'; the form is reflexive in sense, 'they set themselves in readiness'. Radak explains the doubled kaf as absorbing the reflexive tav.

verses.translation_literal: And you, YHWH, God of hosts, God of Israel, awake to punish all the nations; do not show favor to any treacherous workers of iniquity. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And you, LORD, God of hosts, God of Israel, rise! Wake and turn your eyes on all the nations. Show no favor to any who betray in wickedness. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene widens at once, from a house to the whole world. 'YHWH, God of hosts, God of Israel' is the full liturgical title, spoken like a king's roll of titles: the man in the house appeals to the commander of all armies. The sudden mention of 'all the nations' puzzled the tradition. Radak says the verse fits neither what comes before nor after unless read of the future; Meiri reads Saul's men as part of the nations; Malbim has David handing his army back to God.

The KJV's 'heathen' and 'visit' both soften or age the Hebrew. Pakad is 'to attend to, to muster, to punish', the verb a commander uses of an inspection. 'Visit' no longer means that in English. The KJV's 'wicked transgressors' blurs a precise phrase: bogdei aven are those who betray (bagad) in wickedness, treacherous people. 'Selah' marks a pause in the performance and is left untranslated.

philological_notes.note: 'To attend to, muster, call to account'. The KJV 'visit' is an old rendering; here it is a judicial inspection that ends in punishment.
Those who act treacherously, in wickedness; bagad is betrayal of a bond. The KJV 'wicked transgressors' loses the betrayal.

verses.translation_literal: They return at evening, they growl like a dog, and go around the city.
verses.translation_dramatic: Evening comes, and they come back with it. They growl like dogs and prowl the streets of the city.
verses.directors_commentary:
The watchers come back at dusk, when the city closes. The dog here is not a pet: it is the pack that roams the streets after dark, scavenging and growling at the edges of the settlement, an image of contempt in the Bible. The KJV's 'make a noise' is too mild; the verb hamah is a low growl or moan, the sound of a dog or a dove or a troubled heart.

Ibn Ezra notes the irony: dogs are guards of a town, and these men are guards of David's house. Radak and Metzudat David hear the circling as a search for David.

philological_notes.note: To growl, murmur, moan. Used of dogs, doves, the sea and a restless heart; a low sound, not a bark.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, they gush forth with their mouth; swords are on their lips; for who hears?
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen to what pours from their mouths: swords sit on their lips. And they say, "Who is listening?"
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb nava' is what a spring does: it bubbles up. The KJV's 'belch out' (which Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link to speaking) gets the crude, uncontrolled flow, though it adds a vulgarity the Hebrew does not mark. 'Swords on their lips' is the sharpest image in the psalm: speech as weapon, a conventional picture of slander, here literal, since the words are the plot to kill David.

The last clause, 'for who hears?', is the soldiers' own thought: they feel safe because no one will report them. The KJV adds 'say they' as a bracket. In a house under watch, the irony is that someone is listening: Rashi says they say it in their hearts; Radak says David was hearing from inside. It is also, for the audience, the speech of men who do not fear God.

philological_notes.note: To gush, bubble like a spring. Used of speech elsewhere (Ps 19:3 'pours forth speech'). Metzudat Zion links it to that verse.
Swords, in the plural, on the lips: speech as a deadly weapon.

verses.translation_literal: And you, YHWH, laugh at them; you mock all the nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD, you laugh at them. You hold all the nations in scorn.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'and you' answers the 'who hears?' of the last verse: someone does hear, and he laughs. The scene is the same as Psalm 2:4, where the one enthroned in heaven laughs at kings; Meiri names that psalm. The laughter is not amusement but a king's contempt for a rival who cannot succeed.

The KJV turns the present into the future ('shalt laugh', 'shalt have in derision'). The Hebrew imperfect can be either, but the effect is a settled posture: he laughs. 'All the nations' returns from verse 6, so the plotting of one man's enemies is folded into a world drama.

philological_notes.note: To mock, deride; stronger than the laughter of 'sachak'. The pair appears in Psalm 2:4 and 37:13.

verses.translation_literal: His strength, for you I will watch; for God is my refuge.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their strength is great, and still I keep my watch for you, for God is my high place, my stronghold.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew reads 'his strength', not 'my strength', and the English versions that read 'my strength' follow a repair of the text. Taken as it stands, it is difficult. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read 'his' as the enemy's: the strength of my powerful enemy, I will wait on you. Malbim reads it as God's word to David.

The KJV 'wait upon thee' is a good rendering of 'I will watch': the same verb shamar, which in verse 1 names the guards of the house, now names David's own vigil. The watchers watch the house; David watches God. 'Refuge' is misgav, the high place of verse 2, completing the frame. The KJV's 'defence' is vaguer than a tower.

philological_notes.note: 'His strength', in the received text. Many readers emend to 'my strength' as in verse 18; Rashi and Radak keep it and read it of the enemy.
'I will watch'; the same verb as the watchers in verse 1. Metzudat Zion compares it with Gen 37:11.

verses.translation_literal: The God of my loyalty will meet me; God will let me look on my enemies.
verses.translation_dramatic: The God whose faithful love is mine will come to meet me before they do. God will let me look my enemies in the face.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Chesed' is covenant loyalty, the faithful love that keeps a promise, and 'my chesed' means the loyalty owed to me. The KJV's 'mercy' is thin. The verse has a written/read split: the text written is 'his loyalty' (Ketiv), but it is read 'my' (Qere). Radak explains that the written form is the one who does the kindness, God, and the read form is the one who receives it, David; Meiri takes it as 'God, his loyalty will meet me'.

The verb yekademeni is 'to meet, to come before, to anticipate'. The KJV's 'prevent', which in 1611 meant 'go before', is a trap for the modern reader: it now means the opposite. God does not stop David; he comes first, to meet him. The KJV's 'my desire upon mine enemies' adds 'desire', which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew says only 'let me look on my enemies', as a victor looks down. Rashi and Ibn Ezra supply the longing.

philological_notes.note: Written 'his loyalty' (Ketiv), read 'my loyalty' (Qere). Radak: the written form names the giver, the read form the receiver.
To come to meet, to precede. The KJV 'prevent' means 'go before' in 17th-century English.
Those who lie in wait, observers, from shur 'to look'; Metzudat Zion links it to looking.

verses.translation_literal: Do not kill them, lest my people forget; make them wander by your strength and bring them down, our shield, Lord.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not kill them, or my people will forget. Make them wander by your strength. Bring them down, O Lord, our shield.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the surprise of the psalm: a man in danger asks that his enemies not be killed. The reason is memory: the dead are forgotten, and a living ruin is a lesson. Rashi: all the dead are forgotten, so let them lose their wealth and be poor, a vengeance that is remembered for a long time. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the same.

The KJV's 'scatter' is gentler than 'make them wander': hani'emo comes from nua', to totter, drift, be a vagrant, the fate of Cain in Genesis 4. The enemies become beggars. 'Bring them down' means from their high status. 'Our shield' is magen, the small round shield of a soldier; the KJV is right to keep 'shield'. 'Adonai' ends the verse with a note of address, 'my Lord'. 'Chayil' ('by your strength') is military might; Ibn Ezra takes the word here as Israel.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of nua', 'to shake, wander'. Make them vagrants, as with Cain (Gen 4:12). Ibn Ezra reads it as begging for bread.
'Our shield': the small shield of a warrior, used of God as protector.

verses.translation_literal: [The] sin of their mouth, [the] word of their lips, and let them be caught in their pride, and from [the] curse and from [the] lying [that] they recount.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their mouths are their sin, and what their lips shape is the sin itself. So let the trap close on the pride they wear. Let the oaths they swore and the lies they told be the net that holds them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens with a pile of nouns and no verb: the sin of their mouth, the word of their lips. Speak it as an indictment read out in court, each phrase set down like a stone. The KJV smooths it into 'for the sin of their mouth and the words of their lips', which makes the first half a ground for the second. The Hebrew says only that the mouth's sin is the lips' word, and the commentators disagree on how the clause hangs together (Meiri says the order is irregular or a word is missing).

The two nouns at the end carry weight. אָלָה is the oath that carries a curse, and Malbim hears in it the false oaths the enemies swore to confirm their slander. כַּחַשׁ is lying, and also a word for thinness or wasting, which is how Metzudat Zion glosses it. The KJV's 'cursing' flattens אָלָה to swearing in anger. The superscription of the psalm says Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him. 'Let them be caught in their pride' is poetic justice: the hunters are to be hunted in the very thing they boast about.

philological_notes.note: An oath bound by a curse, not simply a curse word. The KJV's 'cursing' blurs the sense of a sworn statement. Malbim takes it as the false oaths they swore to confirm their slander.
Lying, deceit; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'thinness' (רזון), the same root meaning leanness or wasting, a word the commentators play on when they read the verse as a curse of emaciation.

verses.translation_literal: Make an end in wrath, make an end, and there is no them, and let them know that God is ruling in Jacob, to the ends of the earth. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: End them. End them in your fury, end them, until there is nothing of them left to find. And let the world learn it, to the farthest edge of the earth: God rules in Jacob. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The doubled imperative כַּלֵּה כַּלֵּה is a drumbeat; give each word the same weight and let the second fall harder than the first. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear in it a gradual process, 'little by little, and in the end there is no trace of them', while the Hebrew simply repeats the command and then states the result, וְאֵינֵמוֹ, 'and they are not'. The KJV's 'that they may not be' turns that clause into a purpose; the Hebrew states it flatly, which makes it colder and more certain. Note too the old-fashioned rare form אֵינֵמוֹ, with the archaic -מוֹ ending that also appears in verse 13; it gives the line a liturgical weight.

The verse then turns outward. 'God rules in Jacob' is a claim about Israel's God against the gods of the surrounding peoples (Ibn Ezra: the gods of the nations are idols, the God of Israel judges justly), and the point is that his verdict will be seen 'to the ends of the earth'. A tough prayer in a tough age: David is not asking for private revenge but for a public demonstration, which is why the verse is closed by Selah. The word probably marks a pause or a musical lift. Its exact meaning is lost, so the best an actor can do is hold the silence.

philological_notes.note: Piel imperative of כלה, 'to bring to an end, finish off, consume'. Repeated for emphasis. 'Consume' in the KJV suggests burning; the verb is about completion and ending. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear a gradual process: little by little, and in the end they are gone.
'Ruling in Jacob' with ב: God's rule is located inside Israel, as king in the midst of his people, not simply over it. Radak says he supervises Israel more closely than the other nations.

verses.translation_literal: And let them return at evening, they growl like the dog, and go around [the] city.
verses.translation_dramatic: And when evening comes, let them come back, as they did before, growling like dogs, circling the city in the dusk.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse repeats the refrain of verse 7, 'they return at evening, they growl like a dog, they go around the city'. There the dogs were the hunters watching David's house; here the same words come back as a curse. Malbim and Metzudat David both read it as measure for measure: those who prowled the streets at night to kill will prowl them again, but now for food. The KJV's 'make a noise' is too tame for יֶהֱמוּ, which is the growling or moaning of an animal, and the same verb is used for the roaring of the sea and the moaning of a troubled heart. The Hebrew keeps it ambiguous whether this is a threat or an echo.

The dogs are the pariah dogs of an ancient town, half wild, living on scraps and coming out at dusk when the streets empty and the gates are closed. Evening is when the day's watch begins; a city wall, a closed gate and a growling pack outside is a precise image of a hunted man inside and enemies who cannot quite reach him.

philological_notes.note: Dog. In the Bible dogs are scavengers, not pets, and the word is also an insult. The comparison puts the enemies among the lowest of the city's creatures.
To growl, moan, roar. The verb covers the sound of a dog, the sea and a restless heart; Metzudat David reads it here as moaning from hunger-pain.

verses.translation_literal: They, they wander about to eat; if they are not satisfied, then they pass the night.
verses.translation_dramatic: They drift from door to door in search of a meal. And if they are not filled, the night finds them still hungry.
verses.directors_commentary:
הֵמָּה, 'they', opens the line with its own stress. After David's prayer the pronoun points at the enemy and shows them reduced to the same hunger they once inflicted on others. The verb יְנִיעוּן is a Hiphil from נוע, 'to shake, totter, wander', so they are made to roam; Metzudat Zion links it to the exile's 'wanderer and fugitive' (נָע וָנָד).

The last two words split the translations. The KJV has 'grudge', following the sense 'murmur' of לון, and Rashi, Radak and Meiri disagree among themselves about the sense of the conditional clause. I read it with וַיָּלִינוּ as the ordinary verb 'to lodge for the night': they wander for food, and if they are not satisfied they spend the night hungry, as the dogs of verse 15 would. The mood is bleak and a little ironic: the pack that circled the city at dusk is now begging for a scrap.

philological_notes.note: Qere reading, Hiphil of נוע: 'they cause themselves to wander'. The ending -ון is a rare longer form of the imperfect. Metzudat Zion ties it to נָע וָנָד.
Either 'and they spend the night' (לון I) or 'and they murmur' (לון II, as in the KJV 'grudge'). Both readings are old; here the first suits the picture of a hungry night.

verses.translation_literal: And I, I will sing your strength, and I will ring out at morning your covenant loyalty, for you have been a stronghold for me, and a place of flight in [the] day [when] it was narrow for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I will sing. I will sing of your strength, and when the morning comes I will shout your faithful love aloud. For you were my high place, my place to run to, on the day when the walls closed in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here on the first word, וַאֲנִי, 'but I', set against the 'they' of the last three verses. The dogs return at evening; the singer sings at morning. Ibn Ezra notes the contrast exactly: dogs bark at night, the singer sings by day. Let the actor drop the growl and let the voice open up.

Two military words carry the verse: מִשְׂגָּב, a high, inaccessible place, a fortress on a rock, and מָנוֹס, a place to flee to. The KJV's 'defence and refuge' is a harmonised pair that loses the vertical image of the first and the running of the second. In the hills of Judah, the 'high place' is literal: an outcrop a pursuer cannot climb. And צַר־לִי is, literally, 'it was narrow for me': the Hebrew idea of trouble is tightness, a place with no room. חֶסֶד is not 'mercy', as the KJV has it, but covenant loyalty, the faithful commitment a lord owes his people. The morning is the hour of salvation in Hebrew poetry, when the night watch ends and the danger passes.

philological_notes.note: A high, unreachable place, a fortress on a height rather than a defensive wall in general. Radak glosses the same word in verse 2 as a lofty place that cannot be reached.

Covenant loyalty, faithful love that keeps a commitment. 'Mercy' in the KJV implies pity for the guilty; the sense is rather the loyalty of a party who has bound himself. Ibn Ezra sets 'your חסד' here against 'the God of my חסד' in verse 18.
Literally 'it was narrow for me', the verb of tightness, from the same root as צָרָה, 'distress'. The Hebrew sees trouble as lack of room.

token_glosses.gloss: and I will ring out [a song]

verses.translation_literal: My strength, to you I will sing praises, for God [is] my stronghold, the God of my covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: My strength, it is to you I sing. For God is my high place, the God whose faithful love I have known.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse echoes verse 10 almost word for word. There: עֻזּוֹ אֵלֶיךָ אֶשְׁמֹרָה כִּי־אֱלֹהִים מִשְׂגַּבִּי, 'his strength, to you I will keep watch, for God is my stronghold'. Here: עֻזִּי אֵלֶיךָ אֲזַמֵּרָה כִּי־אֱלֹהִים מִשְׂגַּבִּי. 'His strength' has become 'my strength', and 'I will watch' has become 'I will sing'. The watching of the night gives way to the song of the morning. Radak reads exactly this: in the hour of trouble the singer watches and hopes, and when salvation comes he turns to song. Malbim has David waiting for Saul's strength, the kingship, to become his own and then singing to the one who gave it.

The KJV renders מִשְׂגָּב 'defence' here, and חֶסֶד 'mercy', softening the covenant promise into pity. The final phrase אֱלֹהֵי חַסְדִּי, 'the God of my covenant loyalty', is a bold turn: God is defined by what he does for his people. Let the actor finish quietly, with no triumph, only certainty. The verb אֲזַמֵּרָה shares its root with מִזְמוֹר, 'psalm'.

philological_notes.note: To sing praise; the root of מִזְמוֹר, 'psalm'. The ending -ָה is the cohortative of resolve. It replaces אֶשְׁמֹרָה, 'I will watch', of verse 10.
'The God of my covenant loyalty': God is named by the quality he shows. Ibn Ezra reads it as answering 'your covenant loyalty' in verse 17.
